name: Rosedale diet

lead: The Rosedale diet is a low-carbohydrate eating plan designed by physician Ron Rosedale. It is built on his ideas about the hormone leptin and insulin. People who follow it do so for fat loss and a leaner physique, as well as for metabolic health.

It keeps carbohydrates very low, limits protein to a moderate amount and relies on fat for most calories; a T Nation forum post quotes 60 to 65 percent fat and 25 to 30 percent protein for athletic training [3]. Wikipedia reports it has been criticised by science-based medicine commentators, and describes no controlled trials of the diet [1].

paras: Followers cut grains, sugar and starches, set protein limits (unlike many bodybuilding low-carb plans), and take supplements and tests recommended in Rosedale's books [1][2]. Bodybuilders on T Nation discussed it alongside other low-carb plans [3][4].

The plan is described as severely carbohydrate-restrictive and as recommending supplements and many tests [1]. Critics cited by Wikipedia say it lacks a sound scientific basis and that safety and effectiveness are not established [1]. Protein limits differ from usual advice for people building muscle.

angle.text: Followers use it as a fat-loss diet: by minimising carbohydrates they aim to lose body fat, which shows up as a leaner face and body.

lead: The Rosedale diet is a low-carbohydrate fad diet devised by physician Ron Rosedale and based on his views of how leptin and insulin affect the body [1]. People adopt it to lose fat and improve body composition, which supports a leaner appearance.

The plan has two phases with lists of restricted and permitted foods, and recommends supplements and a series of health tests [1]. On T Nation, members discussed it in threads on low-carb eating, with one summarising its macro split as roughly 60 to 65 percent fat and 25 to 30 percent protein [2].

Critic Harriet Hall reviewed the book on Science-Based Medicine in 2015 and said it lacked a scientific basis [1]. Rosedale, Eric Westman and John Konhilas published a 2009 paper, Clinical Experience of a Diet Designed to Reduce Aging [1].

paras: The diet restricts carbohydrates severely, divides into two parts with food lists, and includes supplements and about 16 unconventional annual health checks [1]. Unlike some bodybuilding low-carb plans, it sets limits on protein, a difference noted by a T Nation poster comparing it with another diet [3].

T Nation posters mention the diet in threads on the Anabolic Diet, paleo eating and diabetes [4][5]. One forum member described Rosedale's recommendations for athletic training as 60 to 65 percent fat and 25 to 30 percent protein [2]. Another poster said they thought Rosedale's leptin material was useful but disliked the need to buy supplements [4].

Wikipedia states the diet is not based on sound science and that there is no evidence it is safe or effective, citing Hall's review on Science-Based Medicine [1]. Proponents cite Rosedale's clinical experience and reasoning about leptin and insulin.
No studies found of the diet as a whole beyond a 2009 practitioner report by Rosedale, Westman and Konhilas, Clinical Experience of a Diet Designed to Reduce Aging [1].
